'''''Acorus calamus''''' (also called '''sweet flag''', '''sway''' or '''muskrat root''', among many other common names<ref name=str>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QZAhYVPeRL0C&q=%22Acorus+calamus%22+beewort&pg=PA119 |title=Wildflowers of Iowa Woodlands |page=119 |author1=Sylvan T. Runkel |author2=Alvin F. Bull |publisher=[[University of Iowa Press]] |location=Iowa City, Iowa |orig-date=1979 |year=2009 |access-date=13 December 2011 |isbn=978-1-58729-884-4 }}</ref>) is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]]. It is a tall [[wetland]] [[monocot]] of the family [[Acoraceae]], in the genus ''[[Acorus]].'' Although used in [[traditional medicine]] over centuries to treat [[Gastrointestinal disease|digestive disorders]] and pain, it has no [[evidence-based medicine|clinical evidence]] of safety or efficacy and may be [[toxicity|toxic]] if ingested, and so has been commercially [[ban (law)|banned]] for use in food in the United States.<ref name="drugs">{{cite web |title=Calamus |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/calamus.html |publisher=Drugs.com |access-date=28 January 2019 |date=2018 |archive-date=27 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190327091556/https://www.drugs.com/npp/calamus.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Acorus-calamus1.jpg|thumb|Inflorescence]]
Sweet flag is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]], {{cvt|2|m|in}} tall.<ref name=drugs/> Its leaves resemble those of the [[Iridaceae|iris family]]. Sweet flag consists of tufts of basal leaves that rise from a spreading [[rhizome]].<ref name=drugs/> The leaves are erect yellowish-brown, radical, with pink sheathing at their bases, sword-shaped, flat and narrow, tapering into a long, acute point, and have parallel veins. The leaves have smooth edges, which can be wavy or crimped. The sweet flag can be distinguished from iris and other similar plants by the crimped edges of the leaves, the fragrant odor it emits when crushed, and the presence of a [[spadix (botany)|spadix]].<ref name="hilty">{{cite web |author=John Hilty |url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/wetland/plants/sweetflag.htm |title=Sweet flag |publisher=Wetland Wildflowers of Illinois |access-date=28 January 2019 }}</ref><ref name="rook">{{cite web |url=http://www.rook.org/earl/bwca/nature/aquatics/acorus.html |title=''Acorus americanus'' – Sweet Flag |date=14 April 2004 |website=Rook.Org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060825163223/http://www.rook.org/earl/bwca/nature/aquatics/acorus.html |archive-date=25 August 2006 }}</ref>

Only plants that grow in water bear flowers. The fruit is a berry filled with mucus, which when ripe falls into the water and disperses by floating. The solid, triangular flower-stems rise from the axils of the outer leaves. A semi-erect spadix emerges from one side of the flower stem. The spadix is solid, cylindrical, tapers at each end, and is 5 to 10 cm in length. A covering spathe, as is usual with [[Araceae]], is absent. The spadix is densely crowded with tiny greenish-yellow flowers. Each flower contains six petals and stamens enclosed in a perianth with six divisions, surrounding a three-celled, oblong ovary with a sessile stigma. The flowers are sweetly fragrant.<ref name=hilty/><ref name=rook/> In Europe, it flowers for about a month in late spring or early summer, but does not bear fruit. In Asia, it also fruits sparingly, and propagates itself mainly by growth of its rhizome, forming colonies.

The branched, cylindrical, knobby rhizome is the thickness of a human finger and has numerous coarse fibrous roots below it. The exterior is brown and the interior white.<ref name="botanical.com">{{cite web |author=Grieve M |title=Sedge, Sweet; in A Modern Herbal |access-date=1 April 2017 |url=http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/s/sedges39.html |publisher=Botanical.com |date=2018 }}</ref>

==Range and habitat==
Sweet flag is native to the [[Irtysh]] River valley in Kazakhstan, but has been widely introduced worldwide. Habitats include edges of small lakes, ponds and rivers, marshes, swamps, and other wetlands.<ref name=hilty/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/species/55/ |title=''Acorus calamus'' L.; Native American Ethnobotany |publisher=US Department of Agriculture |date=2003 |access-date=12 May 2021 }}</ref>

==Names and etymology==

In addition to "sweet flag" and "calamus" other common names include '''beewort''', '''bitter pepper root''', '''calamus root''', '''flag root''', '''gladdon''', '''myrtle flag''', '''myrtle grass''', '''myrtle root''', '''myrtle sedge''', '''pine root''', '''sea sedge''', '''sweet cane''', '''sweet cinnamon''', '''sweet grass''', '''sweet myrtle''', '''sweet root''', '''sweet rush''', '''sweet sedge''' and '''wada kaha'''.<ref name="str" /><ref name=drugs/>

The generic name is the [[Latin]] word ''acorus'', which is derived from the Greek άχόρου (áchórou) of [[Dioscorides]] (note different versions of the text have different spellings). The word άχόρου itself is thought to have been derived from the word κόρη (kóri), which means pupil (of an eye), because of the juice from the root of the plant being used as a remedy in diseases of the eye ('darkening of the pupil').<ref>{{cite book |author=Pliny the Elder |title=Naturalis Historia |language=la |trans-title=The Natural History |series=25 |chapter=100 |chapter-url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/L/Roman/Texts/Pliny_the_Elder/25*.html |archive-date=17 February 2024 |access-date=19 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240217004118/https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/L/Roman/Texts/Pliny_the_Elder/25%2A.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Dioscorides, Pedanius |title=Περὶ ὕλης ἰατρικῆς |language=el |trans-title=De Materia Medica |chapter=2 |pages=11, 50–70 |translator=Sprengel, Karl Philipp |year=1829 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Nomina generica, quae Characterem essentialem vel habitum plantae exhibent, optima sunt |url=http://www.scientificlatin.org/philbot/pb240.html |language=la |work=Scientific Latin |date=14 October 2001 |access-date=9 July 2013 |archive-date=11 September 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140911001743/http://www.scientificlatin.org/philbot/pb240.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The specific name ''calamus'' is derived from Greek [[kalamos|κάλαμος]] (kálamos, meaning "reed"), [[cognate]] to Latin ''culmus'' ("stalk") and Old English ''healm'' ("straw"), Arabic قَلَم{{lrm}}{{lrm}} (qálam, "pen"), in turn from [[Proto-Indo European]] ''*kole-mo-'' (thought to mean "grass" or "reed").{{citation needed|date=July 2022}} The name "sweet flag" refers to its sweet scent and its similarity to ''Iris'' species, which have been commonly known as flags in English since at least the late fourteenth century.<ref name=rook/><ref>{{cite web |author=Harper, Douglas |work=Online Etymological Dictionary |title=Flag |url=http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=flag&allowed_in_frame=0 }}</ref>

==History==
The plant was already mentioned in the [[Chester Beatty Medical Papyrus|Chester Beatty papyrus VI]] dating to approximately 1300 BC. The ancient Egyptians rarely mentioned the plant in medicinal contexts, but it was certainly used to make perfumes.<ref name=":2">Manniche, Lisa; An Ancient Egyptian Herbal, p. 74; American University in Cairo Press; Cairo; 2006; {{ISBN|977 416 034 7 }}</ref>

One of the ingredients in [[holy anointing oil]], {{transliteration|hbo|kaneh bosem}} meaning "spiced cane" or "sweet cane", is identified by Robert Sturtevant and Butler Stanton as ''Acorus calamus''.<ref name="Moldenke">{{Cite book |last1=Moldenke |first1=Harold Norman |author-link1=Harold Norman Moldenke |last2=Moldenke |first2=Alma Lance |date=1952 |title=Plants of the Bible |location=New York |publisher=Ronald Press Company |page=40 |oclc=459603419 }}</ref> However, botanists such as [[James A. Duke]] and [[Harold Norman Moldenke]] reject this as it did not grow in [[Ancient Israel and Judah|Ancient Israel]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Duke |first1=James A. |author-link1=James A. Duke |date=1983 |title=Medicinal Plants of the Bible |url=https://archive.org/details/medicinalplantso0000duke |url-access=registration |location=Owerri, Nigeria |publisher=Trado-Medic Books |page=163 |isbn=978-0-932426-23-9 |oclc=9853464 |access-date=27 September 2025 }}</ref><ref name="Moldenke" />

Initially, Europeans confused the identity and medicinal uses of the ''Acorus calamus'' of the Romans and Greeks with their native ''[[Iris pseudacorus]]''. Thus the ''Herbarius zu Teutsch'', published at Mainz in 1485, describes and includes a woodcut of this iris under the name ''Acorus''. This German book is one of three possible sources for the same error in the French ''Le Grant Herbier'', written in 1486, 1488, 1498 or 1508, which was also published in an English translation as the ''[[Grete Herball]]'' by [[Peter Treveris]] in 1526; all of these contain the false identification printed in the ''Herbarius zu Teutsch''.<ref>Rohde, Eleanour Sinclair; ''The Old English Herbals''; Longmans, Green and Co.; 1922; accessed at https://www.gutenberg.org/files/33654/33654-h/33654-h.htm {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924215315/http://www.gutenberg.org/files/33654/33654-h/33654-h.htm |date=24 September 2015 }}</ref> [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner]], writing in 1538, describes 'acorum' as "gladon or a flag, a yelowe floure delyce".<ref>Turner, William; Libellus de re herbaria, pg. Aii; 1538; in Jackson, Benjamin Daydon; Libellus de re herbaria novus, by William Turner, originally pub. in 1538, reprinted in facsimile, p. 36; private print; London; 1877; accessed at https://archive.org/stream/libellusdereherb00turn#page/n36/mode/1up</ref>

The plant was introduced to Britain in the late 16th century. By at least 1596, true ''Acorus calamus'' was grown in Britain, as it is listed in ''The Catalogue'', a list of plants [[John Gerard]] grew in his garden at Holborn. Gerard notes, "It prospereth exceeding well in my garden, but as yet beareth neither flowers nor stalke". Gerard lists the Latin name as ''Acorus verus'', but it is evident there was still doubt about its veracity: in his 1597 herbal he lists the English common name as 'bastard calamus'.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Jackson, Benjamin Daydon |year=1876 |title=A catalogue of plants cultivated in the garden of John Gerard |pages=[https://archive.org/details/mobot31753002733357/page/1 1], 23 |publisher=private printing |location=London |url=https://archive.org/details/mobot31753002733357 }}</ref> [[Carl O. Sauer]] reported that the tuber was already being used by North American Indians at the time of European contact.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sauer |first1=Carl O. |title=Agricultural Origins and Dispersals (Bowman Memorial Lectures) |date=1969 |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology Press |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |page=56 |edition=2nd }}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
[[File:Illustration Acorus calamus0.jpg|thumb|right|Illustration from an 1885 flora by [[Walther Otto Müller]]]]
There are three cytotypic forms distinguished by chromosome number: a diploid form (2n=24), an infertile triploid form (2n=36), and a tetraploid form (see below). The triploid form is the most common and is thought to have arisen relatively recently in the Himalayan region through hybridisation of the diploid with the tetraploid.<ref name="ReferenceB" />

Probably indigenous to most of Asia, the triploid form ''Acorus calamus'' var. ''calamus'' (also known as var. ''vulgaris'' or var. ''verus'') has now been introduced across Europe, Australia, [[New Guinea]], South Africa, [[Réunion]] and North America.<ref name="ReferenceB">Heng, Li (李恒), Guanghua, Zhu (朱光华); and Bogner, Josef; ''Flora of China'', Vol. 23, Acoraceae; Science Press & Missouri Botanical Garden; Beijing & St. Louis; 2010; accessed at http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200027130</ref><ref>{{cite web |work=Tropicos |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |url=http://www.tropicos.org/NameSearch.aspx?name=Acorus+calamus&commonname= |title=''Acorus calamus'' |access-date=9 July 2013 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304195030/http://www.tropicos.org/NameSearch.aspx?name=Acorus+calamus&commonname= |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="apps.kew.org">Govaerts, R.; ''World Checklist of Selected Plant Families: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew''; 2002; http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=2309; accessed 9 July 2013</ref><ref>African Plant Database, ''Acorus calamus''; Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques & South African National Biodiversity Institute; last modified 14 February 2007; http://www.ville-ge.ch/musinfo/bd/cjb/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=30524 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304070657/http://www.ville-ge.ch/musinfo/bd/cjb/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=30524 |date=4 March 2016 }}; accessed 9 July 2013</ref><ref>Euro+Med Plantbase; http://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=77936&PTRefFk=8000000; accessed 9 July 2013</ref><ref>Randall, R.P.; ''The introduced flora of Australia and its weed status''; CRC for Australian Weed Management; Glen Osmond; September 2007; accessed at http://www.agric.wa.gov.au/objtwr/imported_assets/content/hort/intro_flora_australia.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331130020/http://www.agric.wa.gov.au/objtwr/imported_assets/content/hort/intro_flora_australia.pdf |date=31 March 2012 }}</ref><ref>Index de la flore vasculaire de la Réunion; http://www.tela-botanica.org/eflore/BDNFM/2006.01/nn/118; accessed 9 July 2013</ref> The tetraploid form ''Acorus calamus'' var. ''angustatus'' is native throughout Asia, from India to Japan and the Philippines and from Indonesia to Siberia.<ref name="apps.kew.org"/> The diploid form ''[[Acorus americanus]]'' or ''Acorus calamus'' var. ''americanus'' is found in northern subarctic North America and scattered disjunct areas throughout the [[Mississippi Valley]]. It may not be native to some of these areas, Pre-Columbian populations are thought to have dispersed it across parts of the United States.<ref name="apps.kew.org"/><ref name="efloras.org">Thompson, Sue A.; ''Flora of North America'', Acorus; 2000; http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=100307 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130718135345/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=100307 |date=18 July 2013 }}</ref><ref>Gilmore, Melvin R., ''Dispersal By Indians a Factor in the Extension of Discontinuous Distribution of Certain Species of Native Plants'', Papers of the Michigan Academy of Science, Arts, and Letters 13 (1931): 89–94; http://triscience.com/General/dispersal-by-indians-a-factor-in-the-extension-of-discontinuous-distribution-of-certain-species-of-native-plants/doculite_view</ref><ref name=":0" /> Other diploids are found in Mongolia, central Siberia ([[Buryatia]]), [[Gilgit–Baltistan]] in Pakistan, and northern [[Himachal Pradesh]] in India.{{cn|date=September 2025}}

Currently the taxonomic position of the different forms is contested. The comprehensive taxonomic analysis in [[Plants of the World Online]] from 2023 considers all three forms to be distinct varieties of a single species.<ref name="POWO"/> The Flora of North America publication considers the diploid form to be a distinct species; its analysis differentiates North American diploid forms from triploid and tetraploid varieties, and does not take into account the morphology of Asian forms of the diploid variety.<ref name="efloras.org"/> Also, in older literature, the name ''Acorus americanus'' may be used indiscriminately for all forms of ''Acorus calamus'' occurring in North America, irrespective of cytological diversity (i.e. both the diploid and triploid forms).<ref name=efloras.org/> The treatment in the Flora of China from 2010 considers all varieties to be synonyms of a single taxonomically undifferentiated species, since characteristics that are treated as distinctive in the Flora of North America are subject to morphological overlap in Asian specimens.<ref name="ReferenceB"/>

The primary [[Morphology (biology)|morphological]] distinction between the triploid and the North American forms of the diploid is made by the number of prominent leaf veins, the diploid having a prominent midvein with equally raised secondary veins on both sides, the triploid having a single prominent midvein with the secondary veins barely distinct.<ref name=efloras.org/> According to the Flora of China, there is clear overlap in these characteristics and the different [[cytotype]]s are impossible to distinguish morphologically.<ref name="ReferenceB"/> Triploid plants are infertile and show an abortive [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] with a shrivelled appearance. This form will never form fruit (let alone seeds) and can only spread asexually.<ref name=efloras.org/>

The tetraploid variety is usually known as ''Acorus calamus'' var. ''angustatus'' [[Wilibald Swibert Joseph Gottlieb von Besser|Besser]]. A number of synonyms are known, but some of those are contested as to which variety they belong. It is morphologically diverse, with some forms having very broad and some narrow leaves. It is also cytotypically diverse, with an array of different [[karyotype]]s.<ref name="apps.kew.org"/><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Ogra |first1=R. K. |last2=Mohanpuria |first2=Prashant |last3=Sharma |first3=Upendra K. |last4=Sharma |first4=Madhu |last5=Sinha |first5=A. K. |last6=Ahuja |first6=P. S. |title=Indian calamus (''Acorus calamus'' L.): not a tetraploid |journal=Current Science |date=2009 |volume=97 |issue=11 |pages=1644–1647 |jstor=24107305 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Hong |first1=Wang |last2=Wen-Li |first2=L. I. |last3=Zhi-Jian |first3=G. ==Chemistry==

Calamus leaves and rhizomes contain a [[Volatile organic compound|volatile oil]] that gives a characteristic odor and flavor.<ref name=drugs/><ref>{{cite web |title=acorus calamus root oil|url=https://scentsandflavors.com/database/9dbb4ae4-f175-4278-b461-88506075080b |website=scentsandflavors.com |access-date=2 July 2026}}</ref> Major components of the oil are beta-[[asarone]] (as much as 75%), [[methyl isoeugenol]] (as much as 40%) and alpha-asarone, [[saponin]]s, [[lectin]]s, [[sesquiterpenoid]]s, [[lignan]]s, and [[steroid]]s.<ref name=drugs/> [[Phytochemical]]s in the plant vary according to geographic location, plant age, climate, species variety, and plant component [[extract]]ed.<ref name=drugs/><ref name=vpvb>{{cite journal |last1=Streloke |first1=M. |last2=Ascher |first2=K. R. S. |last3=Schmidt |first3=G. H. |last4=Neumann |first4=W. P. |title=Vapor pressure and volatility of β-asarone, the main ingredient of an indigenous stored-product insecticide, ''Acorus calamus'' oil |journal=Phytoparasitica |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=299–313 |year=1989 |doi=10.1007/BF02980759 |bibcode=1989Phyto..17..299S |s2cid=22358687 |display-authors=etal }}</ref><ref name=cceo>{{cite journal |last1=Marongiu |first1=Bruno |last2=Piras |first2=Alessandra |last3=Porcedda |first3=Silvia |last4=Scorciapino |first4=Andrea |title=Chemical Composition of the Essential Oil and Supercritical {{chem|C|O|2}} Extract of ''Commiphora myrrha'' (Nees) Engl. and of ''Acorus calamus'' L. |journal=[[Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry]] |volume=53 |issue=20 |pages=7939–7943 |year=2005 |doi=10.1021/jf051100x |pmid=16190653 |bibcode=2005JAFC...53.7939M }}</ref> Diploids do not contain beta-asarone.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

==Safety and regulations==
''A. calamus'' and products derived from ''A. calamus'' (such as its oil) were banned from use as human food or as a food additive in 1968 by the [[United States Food and Drug Administration]].<ref name=drugs/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfcfr/CFRSearch.cfm?fr=189.110 |title=Substances Generally Prohibited From Direct Addition or Use as Human Food: Calamus and its derivatives |work=Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter B, Part 189 |publisher=Food and Drug Administration |access-date=29 May 2025 |archive-date=16 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161016084712/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfcfr/CFRSearch.cfm?fr=189.110 |url-status=live }}</ref> Although limits on consumption in food or alcoholic beverages (115 [[microgram]]s per day) were recommended in a 2001 ruling by the [[European Commission]], the degree of safe exposure remained undefined.<ref name="ec01">{{cite web |title=Opinion of the Scientific Committee on Food on the presence of beta-asarone in flavourings and other food ingredients with flavouring properties |url=https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/safety/docs/fs_food-improvement-agents_flavourings-out111.pdf |publisher=European Commission, Scientific Committee on Food |access-date=28 January 2019 |date=12 December 2001 |archive-date=29 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190129010432/https://ec.europa.eu/food/sites/food/files/safety/docs/fs_food-improvement-agents_flavourings-out111.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Toxicity===

Although calamus has been used for its fragrance and ingested, it has not been studied by rigorous [[clinical research]].<ref name=drugs/> [[Case report|Individual medical reports]] of toxicity mention severe nausea and prolonged vomiting over many hours following oral uses.<ref name=drugs/> Laboratory studies of its [[extract]]s indicate other forms of toxicity,<ref name=drugs/><ref name=ec01/> due mainly to the [[emesis|emetic]] compound β-[[asarone]].<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal |doi=10.1017/S1479262107390928 |title=Essential oil composition and antimicrobial assay of ''Acorus calamus'' leaves from different wild populations |journal=Plant Genetic Resources: Characterization and Utilization |volume=5 |pages=37–44 |year=2007 |last1=Radušienė |first1=J |last2=Judžentienė |first2=A |last3=Pečiulytė |first3=D |last4=Janulis |first4=V |issue=1 |bibcode=2007PGRCU...5...37R |s2cid=86085313 }}</ref> In Ayurveda, the rhizome is used only after a purification step (''shodhana''),
in which it is boiled in media such as cow's milk. Analytical studies have
reported that this processing significantly reduces the rhizome's β-asarone
content,<ref name="Singh2025">{{cite journal |last1=Singh |first1=Inder Pal |last2=Tanwar |first2=Ankur Kumar |last3=Chatterjee |first3=Debanjan |last4=Lal |first4=Uma Ranjan |title=Medicinal chemistry and detoxification of poisonous plants in traditional medicine: A comprehensive review |journal=Toxicon |date=2025 |volume=258 |article-number=108307 |doi=10.1016/j.toxicon.2025.108307 |pmid=40056954}}</ref><ref name="Chatterjee2024">{{cite journal |last1=Chatterjee |first1=Debanjan |last2=Kumar |first2=Ashutosh |last3=Singh |first3=Inder Pal |title=Qualitative and quantitative studies on the chemical changes during Ayurvedic detoxification process of Acorus calamus Linn. (Indian Vacha) |journal=Phytomedicine Plus |date=2024 |volume=4 |issue=2 |article-number=100574 |doi=10.1016/j.phyplu.2024.100574|doi-access=free }}</ref> an effect attributed largely to
volatilization of the heat-labile compound during prolonged boiling.<ref name="Gholkar2013">{{cite journal |last1=Gholkar |first1=Manasi S. |last2=Mulik |first2=Mandar B. |last3=Laddha |first3=Kirti S. |title=Fate of β-asarone in Ayurvedic Sodhana process of Vacha |journal=Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine |date=2013 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=19–22 |pmid=23741157}}</ref>

Allegedly, the plant is psychoactive ([[hallucinogen]]ic), but for example all experiments with American calamus have been completely unsuccessful, even those involving very high dosages (up to 300 g of rhizomes).<ref>Rätsch, C. (2005) The encyclopedia of psychoactive plants: Ethnopharmacology and its applications. Rochester, Vt: Park Street Press. p. 77, p. 80 </ref>

==Uses==
''A. calamus'' has been an item of trade in many cultures for centuries. It has been used in [[traditional medicine]] for various ailments, and the [[Odor|aroma]] of its [[essential oil]] is used in the perfume industry.<ref name=drugs/> The essence from the rhizome is used as a flavor for foods, alcoholic beverages, and [[bitters]] in Europe.<ref name=ec01/> It was also once used to make candy.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering |last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=340 }}</ref>

=== Food ===
The young stalks can be pulled when under {{cvt|30|cm}}; the inner stems can be eaten raw. The roots can be washed, peeled, cut into small pieces, boiled, and simmered in syrup to make candy.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Elias |first1=Thomas S |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A |title=Edible wild plants: a North American field guide to over 200 natural foods |date=2009 |publisher=Sterling |isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9 |page=133 |oclc=244766414 }}</ref>

===In herbal medicine===
Sweet flag has a long history of use in Chinese, Nepalese, and Indian herbal traditions.<ref name=drugs/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mukherjee |first1=Pulok Kumar |last2=Kumar |first2=Venkatesan |last3=Mal |first3=Mainak |last4=Houghton |first4=Peter J. |title=''Acorus calamus'': Scientific Validation of Ayurvedic Tradition from Natural Resources |journal=Pharmaceutical Biology |date=1 January 2007 |volume=45 |issue=8 |pages=651–666 |doi=10.1080/13880200701538724 |s2cid=55943065 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=O'Neill |first1=Alexander R. |last2=Badola |first2=Hemant K. |last3=Dhyani |first3=Pitamber P. |last4=Rana |first4=Santosh K. |title=Integrating ethnobiological knowledge into biodiversity conservation in the Eastern Himalayas |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |date=December 2017 |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=21 |doi=10.1186/s13002-017-0148-9 |pmid=28356115 |pmc=5372287 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Sweet flag was and is used in [[herbalism]] by the [[Chipewyan people]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Johnson |first=Derek |author2=Linda Kershaw |author3=Andy MacKinnon |author4=Jim Pojar |title=Plants of the Western Boreal Forest & Aspen Parkland |publisher=[[Lone Pine Publishing]] |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-55105-058-4}}{{page needed|date=September 2021 }}</ref>

===Horticulture===
This plant is sometimes used as a pond plant in horticulture.<ref name=hilty/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oudhia |first1=P |title=Rice-acorus intercropping: a new system developed by innovative farmers of Chhattisgarh (India) |journal=International Rice Research Notes |date=June 2002 |volume=27 |issue=1 |page=56 |url=http://www.ejournals.ph/article.php?id=8488 }}</ref> There is at least one tetraploid ornamental [[cultivar]] known; it is usually called 'Variegatus',<ref>{{cite web |work=Missouri Botanical Garden |title=''Acorus calamus'' 'Variegatus' |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/plant-finder/plant-details/kc/a634/acorus-calamus-variegatus.aspx |access-date=9 July 2013 }}</ref> but the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]] recommends calling it 'Argenteostriatus'.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Acorus calamus'' 'Argenteostriatus' |work=Royal Horticultural Society |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=56 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130710030305/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=56 |archive-date=10 July 2013 |access-date=9 July 2013 }}</ref>

=== Insecticide and antifungal ===
{{Further|Asarone}}
The asarone from ''A. calamus'', found most abundantly in the dried and pulverized roots, has been identified as having [[insecticide|insecticidal]] properties.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Angier |first=Bradford |url=https://archive.org/details/fieldguidetoedib00angi/page/224/mode/2up |title=Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=Stackpole Books |year=1974 |isbn=0-8117-0616-8 |location=Harrisburg, PA |page=224 |oclc=799792 |author-link=Bradford Angier }}</ref> β-asarone also exhibits anti-fungal activity by inhibiting ergosterol biosynthesis in ''Aspergillus niger''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Venkatesan |first1=Ramya |last2=Karuppiah |first2=Prakash Shyam |last3=Arumugam |first3=Gnanamani |last4=Balamuthu |first4=Kadalmani |date=10 November 2017 |title=β-Asarone Exhibits Antifungal Activity by Inhibiting Ergosterol Biosynthesis in ''Aspergillus niger'' ATCC 16888 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, India Section B: Biological Sciences |volume=89 |language=en |pages=173–184 |doi=10.1007/s40011-017-0930-4 |s2cid=46005148 |issn=0369-8211 }}</ref> However, asarone's toxicity and carcinogenicity in mammals (including humans) means that it may be difficult to develop any practical medications or insecticides based on it.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/ptr.2650090604 |title=Anthelmintic and pesticidal activity of ''Acorus gramineus'' (Araceae) is associated with phenylpropanoid asarones |year=1995 |last1=Perrett |first1=Sheena |last2=Whitfield |first2=Philip J. |journal=Phytotherapy Research |volume=9 |issue=6 |page=405 |s2cid=84823162 }}</ref>

=== Symbolism ===
According to some interpretations, American poet [[Walt Whitman]] used the plant to represent homoerotic male love because of its [[phallic]] connotations.<ref>{{cite book |last=Herrero-Brasas |first=Juan A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ca4FuDfH-cMC&pg=PA46 |title=Walt Whitman's Mystical Ethics of Comradeship: Homosexuality and the Marginality of Friendship at the Crossroads of Modernity |publisher=SUNY |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-4384-3011-9 |page=46}}</ref >
